pos: n. and v. (mirth made at another's expense; the entertainment the Philistines demanded of a blind Samson, and the fool's amusement in mischief)
etymology: A shortened form of disport — Old French desporter, to carry away, to divert. The Hebrew at Judges 16:25 is tsachaq, to laugh or make sport, the same verb behind the name Isaac; at Proverbs 10:23 it is sechoq, laughter.
biblical_def: Scripture's use of sport is almost entirely dark. At Gaza, “when their hearts were merry, that they said, Call for Samson, that he may make us sport. And they called for Samson out of the prison house; and he made them sport: and they set him between the pillars” (Judges 16:25). Three thousand watched from the roof (Judges 16:27). A blind man, shorn and grinding at a mill, was brought out as the entertainment at a feast to Dagon — and the pillars they set him between were the ones he pulled down. Proverbs names the same instinct in ordinary men: “It is as sport to a fool to do mischief: but a man of understanding hath wisdom” (Proverbs 10:23). The fool is not described as malicious but as amused; harm is his recreation. Proverbs 26:19 exposes the standard excuse: “So is the man that deceiveth his neighbour, and saith, Am not I in sport?” — compared in the previous verse to a madman casting firebrands and arrows. Isaiah turns the word on the mockers of God's people: “Against whom do ye sport yourselves? against whom make ye a wide mouth, and draw out the tongue?” (Isaiah 57:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sport as play, diversion, or mirth — and also mock, contemptuous mirth, and a person made the subject of derision.
webster_full: SPORT, n. That which diverts and makes merry; play; game; diversion.
2. Mock; mockery; contemptuous mirth. Then make sport at me. Judges 16.
3. That with which one plays, or which is driven about.
4. Play; idle jingle. An author who should introduce such a sport of words upon our stage.
SPORT, v.i. To play; to frolic; to wanton. 2. To trifle.
scriptures: Judges 16:25

And it came to pass, when their hearts were merry, that they said, Call for Samson, that he may make us sport. And they called for Samson out of the prison house; and he made them sport: and they set him between the pillars.
Judges 16:27
Now the house was full of men and women; and all the lords of the Philistines were there; and there were upon the roof about three thousand men and women, that beheld while Samson made sport.
Proverbs 10:23
It is as sport to a fool to do mischief: but a man of understanding hath wisdom.
Proverbs 26:19
So is the man that deceiveth his neighbour, and saith, Am not I in sport?
corruption_summary: Cruelty framed as humour has been given a permanent excuse — I was only joking — and Proverbs 26:19 names that excuse by its own words.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 26:18-19 is one of the few places where Scripture quotes the defence and answers it. A man deceives his neighbour, and when confronted says Am not I in sport? — and the Holy Ghost compares him to a madman throwing firebrands, arrows, and death. The excuse is not accepted, and the reason is that the injury is real whatever the intention was. The modern forms are familiar: it was banter, it was a joke, you are too sensitive. Where the mockery is aimed at the weak, at a wife, at a child, or at a brother in Christ, the biblical category is not humour at all. Scripture is not humourless — Elijah on Carmel is devastatingly funny at the expense of Baal — but it never permits amusement purchased with a neighbour's harm.

Judges 16:25 is the most terrible use, and it repays a careful reading of what led to it. Samson had been the strongest man in Israel and had spent his strength on riddles, feasts, women, and vengeance; he ended as a blind entertainer at a pagan festival. The Philistines were sporting with a man and, as they thought, with his God: the whole feast was a sacrifice to Dagon for delivering Samson into their hand. His last prayer asks for strength to be avenged for his two eyes, and the narrator records that the dead he slew at his death were more than they which he slew in his life. Hebrews 11 lists him among the faithful, which is a mercy the chapter itself does not explain.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsachaq, to laugh, make sport — Judges 16:25; sechoq, laughter — Proverbs 10:23; anag, to take delight, sport oneself — Isaiah 57:4.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsachaq — to laugh, mock, make sport; Judges 16:25, and the root of the name Isaac.
Hebrew sechoq — laughter, derision; Proverbs 10:23, the fool's amusement in mischief.
Hebrew anag — to be soft, to sport oneself; Isaiah 57:4, of mockers.
Hebrew zimmah — mischief, a wicked device; the object of the fool's sport.
Old French desporter, to carry away or divert — the source of English disport and sport.
usage: “Call for Samson, that he may make us sport” — a blind man as the feast's entertainment.
“It is as sport to a fool to do mischief” — harm as recreation.
“Am not I in sport?” — the excuse quoted, and refused.

pos: a. (flashing with light; in every occurrence of a weapon — the whetted sword of divine vengeance and the spear of an advancing army)
etymology: From Middle English gliteren, of Norse origin, to shine or sparkle. The Hebrew at Deuteronomy 32:41 is baraq, lightning — the sword is literally the lightning of the sword; at Job 39:23 the same root describes a spear.
biblical_def: The Hebrew behind glittering is baraq, the word for lightning, and the Authorized Version reserves the adjective for weapons. The LORD Himself uses it in the song of Moses: “If I whet my glittering sword, and mine hand take hold on judgment; I will render vengeance to mine enemies, and will reward them that hate me” (Deuteronomy 32:41). Vengeance belongs to God, and the whole passage is quoted twice in the New Testament to take it out of human hands. In Job's speech from the whirlwind the war horse is described smelling the battle: “The quiver rattleth against him, the glittering spear and the shield” (Job 39:23). Nahum uses it for the terrible spectacle of Nineveh's fall: “The horseman lifteth up both the bright sword and the glittering spear: and there is a multitude of slain… and there is none end of their corpses” (Nahum 3:3). And Habakkuk, in his great psalm, turns it into a theophany: “The sun and moon stood still in their habitation: at the light of thine arrows they went, and at the shining of thy glittering spear” (Habakkuk 3:11). The flash of a weapon in sunlight is the image; the point is that it is God's weapon.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines glitter as to shine with a bright, brilliant, or broken light, to gleam — and figuratively to be showy or specious.
webster_full: GLITTERING, ppr. Shining; splendid; brilliant.
GLITTER, v.i. To shine; to sparkle with light; to gleam; to be bright.
The field yet glitters with the pomp of war.
2. To be showy, specious or striking, and hence attractive; as glittering scenes.
GLITTER, n. Brightness; brilliancy; splendor; lustre.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 32:41
If I whet my glittering sword, and mine hand take hold on judgment; I will render vengeance to mine enemies, and will reward them that hate me.
The quiver rattleth against him, the glittering spear and the shield.
Nahum 3:3

The horseman lifteth up both the bright sword and the glittering spear: and there is a multitude of slain, and a great number of carcases; and there is none end of their corpses; they stumble upon their corpses:
Habakkuk 3:11
The sun and moon stood still in their habitation: at the light of thine arrows they went, and at the shining of thy glittering spear.
corruption_summary: Divine vengeance is treated as a defect in the Old Testament's portrait of God, when Scripture makes it the very ground on which private revenge is forbidden.
corruption_paragraphs: The song of Moses is one of the passages most often produced as evidence that the Old Testament God is vindictive, and the New Testament's use of it settles the question the other way. Paul quotes Deuteronomy 32:35 — Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord — in the middle of a passage commanding believers to bless their persecutors, feed their enemies, and overcome evil with good. The doctrine of God's vengeance is the premise of Christian non-retaliation, not a rival to it. A man may leave the matter alone precisely because it will not be left alone; the sword is whetted, and it is not in his hand.

Habakkuk 3 shows what such a God is to a believer under a coming invasion. The prophet has just been told that the Chaldeans are being raised up, has argued with God about it, and has been answered. His psalm describes the LORD marching through the land with a glittering spear, and it ends with the most remarkable statement of faith in the prophets: though the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines, yet I will rejoice in the LORD. The glittering weapon is the same in both directions — terror to the enemy, and to the covenant people the guarantee that judgment is real and is God's.
roots_summary: Hebrew baraq, lightning, and so a flashing blade — Deuteronomy 32:41, Habakkuk 3:11; chanith, a spear — Job 39:23, Nahum 3:3; naqam, vengeance — Deuteronomy 32:41.
roots_lines: Hebrew baraq — lightning; “the lightning of my sword” is the literal sense at Deuteronomy 32:41.
Hebrew chanith — a spear; Job 39:23 and Nahum 3:3.
Hebrew naqam — vengeance; the noun Paul quotes in Romans 12:19.
Hebrew shanan — to whet or sharpen; Deuteronomy 32:41, of the sword made ready.
Middle English gliteren, of Norse origin — the source of the English word.
usage: “If I whet my glittering sword” — literally the lightning of the sword.
“The quiver rattleth against him” — the war horse in the speech from the whirlwind.
“The shining of thy glittering spear” — and the fig tree shall not blossom.

pos: v. (adorned, arrayed; of the harlot's bed, of the LORD adorning Jerusalem as a bride, and of the woman on the scarlet beast)
etymology: From Dutch dekken, to cover, entering English in the sixteenth century. The Hebrew at Ezekiel 16:11 is adah, to ornament; the Greek at Revelation 17:4 is chrusoo, to gild — literally golded with gold and precious stones.
biblical_def: The word traces one of Scripture's most sustained figures. God adorns Jerusalem as a husband adorns a bride: “I decked thee also with ornaments, and I put bracelets upon thy hands, and a chain on thy neck” (Ezekiel 16:11) — the whole chapter describes a foundling girl taken up, washed, clothed, and jewelled by the LORD, until she was exceeding beautiful and prospered into a kingdom. Then the same ornaments are turned against Him. Hosea: “she burned incense to them, and she decked herself with her earrings and her jewels, and she went after her lovers, and forgat me, saith the LORD” (Hosea 2:13). Proverbs shows the strange woman preparing: “I have decked my bed with coverings of tapestry, with carved works, with fine linen of Egypt” (Proverbs 7:16). And the figure reaches its end in the Revelation: the woman on the beast “was arrayed in purple and scarlet colour, and decked with gold and precious stones and pearls, having a golden cup in her hand full of abominations” (Revelation 17:4), and the merchants lament her fall in the same words (Revelation 18:16). Ornament given by God, taken to other lovers, and finally displayed by the great harlot — that is the arc.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines deck as to cover, to overspread, and especially to array, adorn, or embellish with something ornamental.
webster_full: DECKED, pp. Covered; adorned; embellished.
DECK, v.t. To cover; to overspread.
2. To dress the person; ornament; to embellish; to array; applied to persons.
3. To adorn; to beautify; to embellish; as, to deck a bed.
DECKING, ppr. Arraying; adorning. n. Ornament; embellishment.
scriptures: Ezekiel 16:11
I decked thee also with ornaments, and I put bracelets upon thy hands, and a chain on thy neck.
Hosea 2:13

And I will visit upon her the days of Baalim, wherein she burned incense to them, and she decked herself with her earrings and her jewels, and she went after her lovers, and forgat me, saith the LORD.
Proverbs 7:16
I have decked my bed with coverings of tapestry, with carved works, with fine linen of Egypt.
Revelation 17:4
And the woman was arrayed in purple and scarlet colour, and decked with gold and precious stones and pearls, having a golden cup in her hand full of abominations and filthiness of her fornication:
corruption_summary: Adornment is treated either as inherently vain or as beyond criticism; Scripture treats it as a gift, and asks who it is worn for.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors flank this word. The ascetic error reads Ezekiel 16 and Revelation 17 as a condemnation of ornament itself, and produces the recurring Christian suspicion of beauty, colour, and craftsmanship — a suspicion the tabernacle chapters flatly contradict, with their gold, blue, purple, scarlet, and precious stones commanded by God. The permissive error refuses the question altogether: what a woman wears is nobody's business, and any comment is control. Ezekiel 16 will not allow either. The ornaments were God's gift and they were genuinely beautiful; the sin was that she took what He gave and wore it for other lovers.

Peter and Paul both take up the subject and neither forbids adornment; both relocate it. Let it not be the outward adorning of plaiting the hair and wearing of gold, but the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible — a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price. Peter's argument is not that jewellery is wicked but that it is the wrong investment, and he uses the vocabulary of value to say so. The question Scripture asks about ornament is never how much but for whom, which is why Revelation 17 is so devastating: the great harlot is decked in exactly the materials of the sanctuary, and holds a golden cup full of abominations.
roots_summary: Hebrew adah, to ornament — Ezekiel 16:11, Hosea 2:13; chatab, to deck or carve — Proverbs 7:16; Greek chrusoo, to gild — Revelation 17:4, 18:16.
roots_lines: Hebrew adah — to pass on, and so to deck or ornament; Ezekiel 16:11 and Hosea 2:13.
Hebrew adi — ornaments, jewellery; the noun of the same root.
Greek chrusoo — to gild, to adorn with gold; Revelation 17:4 and 18:16.
Greek peribalo — to array or clothe about; the companion verb in Revelation 17:4.
Dutch dekken, to cover — the source of the English word.
usage: “I decked thee also with ornaments” — a foundling girl adorned by the LORD.
“She decked herself… and went after her lovers, and forgat me” — the gift turned.
“Decked with gold and precious stones and pearls” — the sanctuary's materials on the harlot.

pos: v. (past tense of crow; in all four Gospels, of the cock that sounded at the moment of Peter's third denial)
etymology: From Old English crawan, to crow — imitative of the sound. Unrelated to the seafaring noun crew. The Greek is phoneo, to make a sound or call out — the same verb used of a man calling, so that the cock is said to speak.
biblical_def: Every Gospel records it, which is itself remarkable, since the four writers select very different material. Matthew: “Then began he to curse and to swear, saying, I know not the man. And immediately the cock crew” (Matthew 26:74). Mark, whose account is traditionally Peter's own, is the most exact: “And the second time the cock crew. And Peter called to mind the word that Jesus said unto him, Before the cock crow twice, thou shalt deny me thrice. And when he thought thereon, he wept” (Mark 14:72). Luke adds the detail that breaks the reader: “And immediately, while he yet spake, the cock crew” (Luke 22:60), and then “the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter” (Luke 22:61). John records it with characteristic brevity: “Peter then denied again: and immediately the cock crew” (John 18:27). The bird knew nothing. It sounded because dawn was coming, as it had every morning of Peter's life, and by the appointment of God it sounded on the exact syllable of a prophecy made hours earlier. The most ordinary noise in Jerusalem became the instrument of a man's restoration.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives crew as the past tense of crow, and defines crow as to cry as a cock, in joy, gaiety, or defiance.
webster_full: CREW, pret. of crow. The cock crew.
CROW, v.i. To cry or make a noise as a cock, in joy, gaiety or defiance.
The cock crew. Matt. 26.
2. To boast in triumph; to vaunt; to vapor; to swagger.
COCK, n. The male of birds, particularly of gallinaceous or domestic fowls.
scriptures: Matthew 26:74
Then began he to curse and to swear, saying, I know not the man. And immediately the cock crew.
Mark 14:72
And the second time the cock crew. And Peter called to mind the word that Jesus said unto him, Before the cock crow twice, thou shalt deny me thrice. And when he thought thereon, he wept.
Luke 22:61
And the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter. And Peter remembered the word of the Lord, how he had said unto him, Before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice.
John 18:27
Peter then denied again: and immediately the cock crew.
corruption_summary: The differences among the four accounts are cited as proof of contradiction, and the doctrine actually at stake — a fall foreknown and a restoration prepared — is passed over.
corruption_paragraphs: The standard critical objection is that Mark has the cock crow twice and the others once, and that the accounts therefore contradict. The observation is accurate and the conclusion does not follow. Mark preserves the fuller form of the saying — before the cock crow twice — and the other three give the shorter and more idiomatic form; a cock crowing twice has certainly crowed. Independent witnesses reporting a shared event with different levels of detail are the ordinary mark of testimony rather than of collusion, and it is worth noting that the account least flattering to Peter is the one traditionally taken down from Peter himself.

What the crowing establishes is more important than the arithmetic. Our Lord told Peter in advance that Satan had desired to have him, that He had prayed for him that his faith fail not, and that when he was converted he should strengthen his brethren — the fall foreknown and the restoration promised in the same breath. Peter's denial was therefore not the collapse of a plan but a passage inside one, and the cock was set to sound at its end so that the word spoken would be remembered. Judas also failed that night and went out and hanged himself; Peter went out and wept bitterly, and the difference between the two is the difference between the sorrow of the world and godly sorrow.
roots_summary: Greek phoneo, to make a sound, call out — the verb of the cock in all four Gospels; alektor, a cock; aparneomai, to deny utterly — the verb of Peter's denial.
roots_lines: Greek phoneo — to utter a sound, to call; used of the cock, and of a man calling out.
Greek alektor — a cock; the bird named in all four accounts.
Greek aparneomai — to deny utterly, disown; Matthew 26:34 and the parallels.
Greek emblepo — to look intently upon; Luke 22:61, of the Lord's look.
Old English crawan — to crow; imitative, and unrelated to the seafaring noun.
usage: “Immediately the cock crew” — recorded by all four evangelists.
“The Lord turned, and looked upon Peter” — and Peter remembered.
The most ordinary noise in Jerusalem, appointed to the syllable.

pos: v. (enrolled for taxation; the imperial census that moved a carpenter and his espoused wife ninety miles to Bethlehem)
etymology: From Latin taxare, to appraise or charge, through Old French taxer. The Greek at Luke 2:1 is apographo, to register or enrol — a census for the purpose of taxation; the Hebrew at 2 Kings 23:35 is arak, to assess.
biblical_def: Luke opens the nativity with an imperial decree: “And it came to pass in those days, that there went out a decree from Caesar Augustus, that all the world should be taxed” (Luke 2:1). The Greek word is not the collection of a tax but the enrolment for one, and Luke records the mechanism precisely: “And all went to be taxed, every one into his own city” (Luke 2:3), which is why Joseph, of the house and lineage of David, went up to Bethlehem, “To be taxed with Mary his espoused wife, being great with child” (Luke 2:5). Seven hundred years earlier Micah had named the town: “But thou, Bethlehem Ephratah, though thou be little among the thousands of Judah, yet out of thee shall he come forth unto me that is to be ruler in Israel; whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting” (Micah 5:2). The most powerful man alive issued an order about revenue, and the order delivered a pregnant woman to a specific village in a distant province at a specific week. The other use of the word is grimmer: Jehoiakim “taxed the land to give the money according to the commandment of Pharaoh” (2 Kings 23:35), a puppet king raising tribute from his own people.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines tax as a rate or sum imposed on persons or property for public use — and cites the Luke text for the sense of enrolment.
webster_full: TAXED, pp. Rated; assessed; charged; enrolled.
TAX, v.t. To lay, impose or assess upon citizens a certain sum of money or amount of property, to be paid to the public treasury.
2. To enroll or register, as for taxation. All the world should be taxed. Luke 2.
3. To load with a burden or burdens.
4. To accuse; to charge; as, to tax a man with pride.
scriptures: Luke 2:1
And it came to pass in those days, that there went out a decree from Caesar Augustus, that all the world should be taxed.
Luke 2:3
And all went to be taxed, every one into his own city.
Luke 2:5
To be taxed with Mary his espoused wife, being great with child.
Micah 5:2

But thou, Bethlehem Ephratah, though thou be little among the thousands of Judah, yet out of thee shall he come forth unto me that is to be ruler in Israel; whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting.
corruption_summary: Luke's census is used as the standard argument against the Gospels' historical reliability, and the providence it displays is dismissed with it.
corruption_paragraphs: The census of Luke 2 is the most-attacked historical claim in the Gospels: the objection is that Quirinius governed Syria in AD 6, that no empire-wide enrolment under Augustus is otherwise attested, and that Romans did not require men to travel to ancestral towns. Each point has a serious answer — the Greek of Luke 2:2 admits the rendering this taxing was before that made when Cyrenius was governor; Augustus records three general censuses in his own Res Gestae; and Egyptian papyri do attest orders requiring people to return to their home districts for enrolment. Luke is elsewhere so precise about titles, provinces, and offices that the burden of proof is not lightly assigned to him.

The doctrine at stake is the one Luke is actually making. An emperor in Rome, pursuing revenue and concerned with nothing else, moved a poor couple from Nazareth to Bethlehem at exactly the right week to fulfil a prophecy written seven centuries earlier by a minor prophet in a village he had never heard of. Augustus was not consulted about this and did not consent to it; Proverbs says the king's heart is in the hand of the LORD, and Luke 2 is the demonstration. God governs the world by means, and the means are frequently the ordinary self-interested machinery of states — which is a great comfort to believers who live under governments that do not know them.
roots_summary: Greek apographo, to enrol or register — Luke 2:1, 2:3, 2:5; apographe, the enrolment itself — Luke 2:2; Hebrew arak, to assess — 2 Kings 23:35.
roots_lines: Greek apographo — to write off, enrol, register for taxation; the verb throughout Luke 2.
Greek apographe — the registration or census; Luke 2:2 and Acts 5:37.
Greek dogma — a decree; Luke 2:1, of Caesar's order.
Greek oikoumene — the inhabited world, the empire; “all the world should be taxed.”
Hebrew arak — to arrange, assess; 2 Kings 23:35, of Jehoiakim's levy for Pharaoh.
usage: “A decree from Caesar Augustus, that all the world should be taxed” — the nativity begins with revenue.
“To be taxed with Mary his espoused wife, being great with child” — ninety miles at the wrong time.
“But thou, Bethlehem Ephratah” — named seven centuries before the decree.

pos: v. and a. (put away from a marriage; regulated for the priesthood, for vows, and addressed directly by our Lord in the Sermon on the Mount)
etymology: From Latin divortium, a separation, from divertere, to turn aside. The Hebrew at Leviticus 21:14 is gerushah, a woman driven out, from garash, to expel; the Greek at Matthew 5:32 is apoluo, to release or put away.
biblical_def: The Mosaic law did not institute divorce; it regulated a practice already in existence and restricted its consequences. A priest might not marry a divorced woman: “A widow, or a divorced woman, or profane, or an harlot, these shall he not take: but he shall take a virgin of his own people to wife” (Leviticus 21:14), the high priest being held to a stricter standard than the congregation. A divorced woman's vows stood on her own head rather than a husband's or father's: “every vow of a widow, and of her that is divorced, wherewith they have bound their souls, shall stand against her” (Numbers 30:9) — a provision that recognises her as a legal person in her own right. Our Lord addresses the matter directly: “whosoever shall put away his wife, saving for the cause of fornication, causeth her to commit adultery: and whosoever shall marry her that is divorced committeth adultery” (Matthew 5:32). When pressed on Deuteronomy 24 He went behind Moses to the creation ordinance: they are no more twain but one flesh, “What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder” (Matthew 19:6) — and said Moses suffered it for the hardness of their hearts, but from the beginning it was not so.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines divorce as a legal dissolution of the bond of matrimony, and notes the distinction between total dissolution and separation from bed and board.
webster_full: DIVORCED, pp. Separated from a husband or wife by law; parted.
DIVORCE, n. A legal dissolution of the bonds of matrimony, or the separation of husband and wife by a judicial sentence.
2. The separation of a married woman from the bed and board of her husband.
3. Separation; disunion of things closely united.
DIVORCE, v.t. To dissolve the marriage contract, and thus to separate husband and wife.
scriptures: Matthew 19:6
Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.
Matthew 5:32
But I say unto you, That whosoever shall put away his wife, saving for the cause of fornication, causeth her to commit adultery: and whosoever shall marry her that is divorced committeth adultery.
Leviticus 21:14
A widow, or a divorced woman, or profane, or an harlot, these shall he not take: but he shall take a virgin of his own people to wife.
Numbers 30:9
But every vow of a widow, and of her that is divorced, wherewith they have bound their souls, shall stand against her.
corruption_summary: No-fault divorce has made marriage terminable at will, and the church has largely followed the culture into treating it as a private and reversible arrangement.
corruption_paragraphs: The legal revolution of the last sixty years replaced fault-based divorce with dissolution on demand, and the practical result is that marriage is now the only contract in Western law that either party may void unilaterally without cause. Our Lord's teaching runs directly against it. Asked which grounds were sufficient — the standing rabbinic debate — He declined to argue about grounds and went to the creation ordinance: God made them male and female, a man shall leave father and mother and cleave to his wife, and they two shall be one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder assumes a joining that man did not perform and therefore cannot dissolve at pleasure.

Scripture is not silent about the exceptions, and pastoral honesty requires naming them: our Lord excepts fornication, and Paul in 1 Corinthians 7 addresses the departure of an unbelieving spouse. The confessional Reformed position has held those two grounds and refused to multiply them. What the tradition has also insisted on, and what is most often neglected, is the direction of Christ's concern in Matthew 5:32 — He speaks of what a man's putting away does to her. In a society where a discarded wife had almost no means of support, the sin He names is the injury done by the stronger party to the weaker, and that emphasis should govern how the church handles these cases still.
roots_summary: Hebrew gerushah, a woman driven out — Leviticus 21:14; garash, to expel; kerithuth, a cutting off, a bill of divorcement — Deuteronomy 24:1; Greek apoluo, to release — Matthew 5:32.
roots_lines: Hebrew gerushah — a woman put away; Leviticus 21:14 and Numbers 30:9.
Hebrew garash — to drive out, expel; the root of the noun.
Hebrew sepher kerithuth — a bill of cutting off; the writing of Deuteronomy 24:1.
Greek apoluo — to loose from, release, put away; Matthew 5:32 and 19:3.
Greek chorizo — to separate; Matthew 19:6, “let not man put asunder.”
usage: “What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder” — the creation ordinance.
“From the beginning it was not so” — our Lord going behind Moses to Genesis.
“Every vow… shall stand against her” — the divorced woman as a legal person.

pos: n. (outward conduct and bearing; a qualification for the eldership, a standard for aged women, and the thing David changed before Achish)
etymology: From behave — be- intensive plus have, in the old sense of bearing or holding oneself. The Greek at 1 Timothy 3:2 is kosmios, orderly and well-arranged, from kosmos, order; at Titus 2:3 it is katastema, demeanour or deportment.
biblical_def: Paul makes outward bearing a formal qualification for office: “A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach” (1 Timothy 3:2). The Greek kosmios is the adjective of kosmos, order — the same word behind the universe as an ordered whole. An elder's life is to be arranged rather than chaotic, and the requirement stands in a list of things any congregation can actually observe. Titus applies the parallel standard to older women: “The aged women likewise, that they be in behaviour as becometh holiness, not false accusers, not given to much wine, teachers of good things” (Titus 2:3), where katastema means settled demeanour — the bearing a person has when nothing in particular is happening. Against these stands a strange episode: fleeing Saul and recognised in Gath, “he changed his behaviour before them, and feigned himself mad in their hands, and scrabbled on the doors of the gate, and let his spittle fall down upon his beard” (1 Samuel 21:13). The psalm David wrote about that day begins “I will bless the LORD at all times” (Psalm 34:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines behavior as manner of behaving, conduct, deportment, and course of life with respect to morals.
webster_full: BEHAVIOR, n. Manner of behaving, whether good or bad; conduct; manners; carriage of one's self, with respect to propriety or morals; deportment.
It expresses external appearance or action; sometimes in a particular character; more generally in the common duties of life.
2. Conduct; course of life.
To be upon one's behavior, is to be in a state of trial, in which something important depends on propriety of conduct.
BEHAVE, v.t. To restrain; to govern; to subdue.
scriptures: 1 Timothy 3:2
A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach;
Titus 2:3
The aged women likewise, that they be in behaviour as becometh holiness, not false accusers, not given to much wine, teachers of good things;
1 Samuel 21:13
And he changed his behaviour before them, and feigned himself mad in their hands, and scrabbled on the doors of the gate, and let his spittle fall down upon his beard.
Psalm 34:1
A Psalm of David, when he changed his behaviour before Abimelech; who drove him away, and he departed. I will bless the LORD at all times: his praise shall continually be in my mouth.
corruption_summary: Character is now assessed by declared belief and stated intention, and Paul assesses it by observable conduct that a congregation can check.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern instinct is that the inner life is the real person and outward conduct is a performance that may or may not represent it — so a man is judged by what he affirms and how he understands himself. Paul's qualification lists work the other way. Every item in 1 Timothy 3 is externally verifiable: whether he is the husband of one wife, whether he is given to wine, whether he is a striker, whether his children are in subjection, whether he has a good report of them which are without. Of good behaviour belongs to that list, and it is there because a church calling a man to office is not equipped to read his heart and is entirely equipped to watch his life.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word itself. The principle to recover is the New Testament's confidence in observable conduct, and its patience. Titus 2:3 uses katastema, settled demeanour, and pairs it with a positive charge — aged women are to be teachers of good things, that they may teach the young women. The passage assumes a congregation in which generations are in contact and the older are watched by the younger. That structure is where behaviour becomes instruction, and it cannot be replaced by a curriculum. David's morning in Gath is a reminder that even a man after God's own heart had days he had to write a psalm about afterward.
roots_summary: Greek kosmios, orderly — 1 Timothy 3:2; kosmos, order, the universe; katastema, demeanour — Titus 2:3; Hebrew taam, taste or discretion — 1 Samuel 21:13.
roots_lines: Greek kosmios — orderly, well arranged; 1 Timothy 3:2, and of women's apparel in 2:9.
Greek kosmos — order, arrangement, and so the ordered universe; the root of kosmios.
Greek katastema — settled demeanour, deportment; Titus 2:3, its only New Testament occurrence.
Greek hieroprepes — as becometh holiness, priestly in bearing; the standard set in the same verse.
Hebrew taam — taste, judgment, discretion; 1 Samuel 21:13, what David changed.
usage: “Of good behaviour” — kosmios, a life arranged rather than chaotic.
“In behaviour as becometh holiness” — settled demeanour, and then teaching.
“He changed his behaviour before them” — and wrote Psalm 34 about the day.

pos: a. (privately knowing, in on a secret; of Shimei's own heart against him, and of Sapphira's knowledge of her husband's lie)
etymology: From Latin privatus, private, through Old French prive. The Hebrew idiom at 1 Kings 2:44 is yada levabeka, thy heart knoweth; the Greek at Acts 5:2 is sunoida, to know together with another — the root of English conscience.
biblical_def: To be privy to a thing is to share the knowledge of it, and Scripture uses the word where that shared knowledge is guilt. Solomon dismisses Shimei with it: “Thou knowest all the wickedness which thine heart is privy to, that thou didst to David my father: therefore the LORD shall return thy wickedness upon thine own head” (1 Kings 2:44). No witnesses are called; the man's own heart is the record. The decisive occurrence is in Acts: Ananias “kept back part of the price, his wife also being privy to it, and brought a certain part, and laid it at the apostles' feet” (Acts 5:2). Sapphira did not carry the money, did not make the speech, and did not tell the lie in that scene — she knew. Three hours later she was given her own opportunity to tell the truth and repeated the lie, and Peter's question to her is the whole doctrine: how is it that ye have agreed together to tempt the Spirit of the Lord? The Greek sunoida — to know along with — is the root of conscience, and it is exactly the point: knowing another's sin and consenting to it makes the knower a party to it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines privy as private or secret, and particularly as privately knowing, admitted to the participation of knowledge with another of a secret transaction.
webster_full: PRIVY, a. Private; pertaining to some person exclusively; assigned to private uses; not public.
2. Secret; clandestine; not open or public; as a privy attempt to kill one.
3. Privately knowing; admitted to the participation of knowledge with another of a secret transaction.
His wife also being privy to it. Acts 5.
PRIVITY, n. Private knowledge; joint knowledge with another of a private concern, which is often supposed to imply consent or concurrence.
scriptures: Acts 5:2
And kept back part of the price, his wife also being privy to it, and brought a certain part, and laid it at the apostles' feet.
Acts 5:3
But Peter said, Ananias, why hath Satan filled thine heart to lie to the Holy Ghost, and to keep back part of the price of the land?
1 Kings 2:44

The king said moreover to Shimei, Thou knowest all the wickedness which thine heart is privy to, that thou didst to David my father: therefore the LORD shall return thy wickedness upon thine own head;
Ezekiel 21:14

Thou therefore, son of man, prophesy, and smite thine hands together, and let the sword be doubled the third time, the sword of the slain: it is the sword of the great men that are slain, which entereth into their privy chambers.
corruption_summary: Complicity is treated as innocence so long as one did not act, and Acts 5 assigns Sapphira the same judgment as the man who spoke.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern reckoning of guilt is heavily weighted toward action: the one who lies is culpable, the one who knew and said nothing is at most awkwardly placed. Acts 5 does not read that way. Sapphira's only recorded act before her examination is knowing, and Luke marks it deliberately — his wife also being privy to it. When she was questioned she had a full opportunity to break with the lie, and she repeated it. Peter names the sin as agreement: How is it that ye have agreed together to tempt the Spirit of the Lord? The word Webster chose for the definition is exact — privity implies consent or concurrence.

Two guards belong here. First, this is not a warrant for treating every person near a sin as equally guilty; Scripture's categories are agreement and consent, not proximity, and the wife who is deceived is a victim rather than a party. Second, the sin was never the withholding. Peter says plainly: whiles it remained, was it not thine own? They could have given nothing, or a tenth, or the whole. What they did was construct a public appearance of total consecration while keeping back part — and they did it together. The judgment fell at the founding of the church, and great fear came upon all the church, and upon as many as heard these things.
roots_summary: Greek sunoida, to know together with — Acts 5:2; suneidesis, conscience, from the same root; nosphizomai, to keep back for oneself — Acts 5:2; Latin privatus, private.
roots_lines: Greek sunoida — to know along with another; Acts 5:2, rendered being privy to.
Greek suneidesis — conscience; formed from the same root, knowledge held with oneself.
Greek nosphizomai — to set apart for oneself, embezzle; Acts 5:2 and Titus 2:10.
Hebrew yada — to know; 1 Kings 2:44, of the heart that is its own witness.
Latin privatus, private — the source of English privy and privity.
usage: “His wife also being privy to it” — Luke marks the knowledge as the participation.
“Thine heart is privy to” — no witness called but the man's own heart.
Sunoida, to know along with — the root of the word conscience.

pos: v. (past of strike; of the LORD striking the child of David and Bathsheba, of Peter's sword in the garden, and of the blows on our Lord's blindfolded face)
etymology: From Old English strican, to stroke, rub, or go. The Hebrew at 2 Samuel 12:15 is nagaph, to smite or plague; the Greek at Matthew 26:51 is patasso, to strike, and at Luke 22:64 tupto, to beat repeatedly.
biblical_def: The word falls in three heavy places. After Nathan's parable and David's confession: “And Nathan departed unto his house. And the LORD struck the child that Uriah's wife bare unto David, and it was very sick” (2 Samuel 12:15). The narrator does not soften the agency, and neither did David, who fasted and lay all night upon the earth for seven days and then washed, anointed himself, and worshipped — saying he would go to the child though the child would not return to him. The second is in Gethsemane: “one of them which were with Jesus stretched out his hand, and drew his sword, and struck a servant of the high priest's, and smote off his ear” (Matthew 26:51). John names the swordsman Peter and the servant Malchus; Luke records that our Lord touched the ear and healed him — the last miracle before the cross, performed on a man who had come to arrest Him. The third is the mockery in the high priest's hall: “when they had blindfolded him, they struck him on the face, and asked him, saying, Prophesy, who is it that smote thee?” (Luke 22:64). They demanded a prophecy from the One of whom Isaiah had prophesied, I hid not my face from shame and spitting.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives struck as the past tense and participle of strike, and defines strike as to touch or hit with some force, either with the hand or an instrument.
webster_full: STRUCK, pret. and pp. of strike.
STRIKE, v.t. To touch or hit with some force, either with the hand or an instrument; to smite; to give a blow to.
2. To dash; to throw with a quick motion.
3. To stamp; to impress; to coin; as, to strike coin at the mint.
4. To punish; to afflict; to smite. To punish; to afflict; to smite. The Lord struck the child. 2 Sam. 12.
scriptures: 2 Samuel 12:15
And Nathan departed unto his house. And the LORD struck the child that Uriah's wife bare unto David, and it was very sick.
Matthew 26:51
And, behold, one of them which were with Jesus stretched out his hand, and drew his sword, and struck a servant of the high priest's, and smote off his ear.
Luke 22:64
And when they had blindfolded him, they struck him on the face, and asked him, saying, Prophesy, who is it that smote thee?
Isaiah 50:6
I gave my back to the smiters, and my cheeks to them that plucked off the hair: I hid not my face from shame and spitting.
corruption_summary: Divine agency in affliction is edited out of texts that state it plainly, and the comfort those texts actually offer goes with it.
corruption_paragraphs: 2 Samuel 12:15 says the LORD struck the child, and modern readers commonly soften it to permission, natural causes, or the working out of consequences. The narrator will not have it, and neither will the rest of Scripture — I kill, and I make alive; I wound, and I heal. The doctrine is not that God is capricious; the same chapter shows a specific sin, a specific prophetic word, a specific judgment announced in advance, and a specific forgiveness granted before the judgment fell: The LORD also hath put away thy sin; thou shalt not die. Removing God's agency to protect His reputation removes the God who can be prayed to about the affliction, which is exactly what David did for seven days.

The garden and the hall show the other direction. Peter struck a blow in defence of Christ and was rebuked for it — put up again thy sword into his place — and the wound he made was the last thing Christ healed before He was bound. Then Christ Himself was struck, blindfolded, and mocked with a demand to prophesy, and He answered nothing. The church has always read these two scenes together: the kingdom does not advance by the sword of its defenders, and its King established it by receiving blows He could have prevented with a word.
roots_summary: Hebrew nagaph, to smite or plague — 2 Samuel 12:15; Greek patasso, to strike — Matthew 26:51; tupto, to beat — Luke 22:64; rapisma, a blow with the palm — John 18:22.
roots_lines: Hebrew nagaph — to strike, smite, plague; 2 Samuel 12:15 and Exodus 12:23.
Greek patasso — to strike, smite; Matthew 26:51, of Peter's sword.
Greek tupto — to beat repeatedly; Luke 22:64, of the blows in the hall.
Greek rapisma — a blow with the open hand; John 18:22, of the officer who struck Him.
Old English strican — to stroke or go; the source of the English verb.
usage: “The LORD struck the child” — the narrator does not soften the agency.
“Struck a servant of the high priest's” — and Christ healed the wound.
“They struck him on the face… Prophesy, who is it that smote thee?”

pos: a. and v. (killed without the shedding of blood; one of the four abstentions the Jerusalem council laid on Gentile believers)
etymology: From Latin strangulare, to choke, through Old French estrangler. The Greek at Acts 15:20 is pniktos, choked or throttled — the adjective for an animal killed without draining its blood.
biblical_def: Three of the four occurrences belong to one decision. The council at Jerusalem, having settled that Gentiles are not to be circumcised or put under the law of Moses for salvation, wrote to them: “that they abstain from pollutions of idols, and from fornication, and from things strangled, and from blood” (Acts 15:20), and in the letter itself, “That ye abstain from meats offered to idols, and from blood, and from things strangled, and from fornication: from which if ye keep yourselves, ye shall do well” (Acts 15:29). James repeats the four to Paul years later (Acts 21:25). A strangled animal is one killed without the blood being drained, and the prohibition therefore belongs with the one beside it. Its ground is older than Moses: “But flesh with the life thereof, which is the blood thereof, shall ye not eat” (Genesis 9:4), given to Noah for all mankind, and explained in Leviticus — “the life of the flesh is in the blood: and I have given it to you upon the altar to make an atonement for your souls” (Leviticus 17:11). Nahum uses the word of a lion: he “strangled for his lionesses” (Nahum 2:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines strangle as to choke, to suffocate, to destroy life by stopping respiration — and notes the scriptural prohibition of things strangled.
webster_full: STRANGLED, pp. Choked; suffocated.
STRANGLE, v.t. To choke; to suffocate; to destroy life by stopping respiration.
Our Saviour was strangled by the cross.
2. To suppress; to hinder from birth or appearance.
STRANGLING, ppr. Choking; suffocating; suppressing.
scriptures: Acts 15:20
But that we write unto them, that they abstain from pollutions of idols, and from fornication, and from things strangled, and from blood.
Acts 15:29
That ye abstain from meats offered to idols, and from blood, and from things strangled, and from fornication: from which if ye keep yourselves, ye shall do well. Fare ye well.
Genesis 9:4
But flesh with the life thereof, which is the blood thereof, shall ye not eat.
Leviticus 17:11
For the life of the flesh is in the blood: and I have given it to you upon the altar to make an atonement for your souls: for it is the blood that maketh an atonement for the soul.
corruption_summary: The four abstentions are read either as a permanent food law or as pure social diplomacy, and the doctrine underneath them — the sanctity of blood — is missed either way.
corruption_paragraphs: Two readings of Acts 15 have long competed. One takes the four abstentions as binding dietary law still, which sits awkwardly with Paul's own teaching in Romans 14 and 1 Corinthians 8 that no meat is unclean of itself. The other treats them as purely diplomatic — concessions to Jewish sensibilities in mixed congregations, with no doctrinal content. Neither is adequate. Fornication in the same list is not a matter of table fellowship, and the blood prohibition is not Mosaic in origin: it was given to Noah, for all humanity, before Abraham and before Sinai. The council is naming things that predate the law it has just declared not binding for salvation.

The doctrinal weight is in Leviticus 17:11. Blood is prohibited because the life of the flesh is in the blood and because God assigned it to the altar for atonement. To treat blood as ordinary food is to treat as common the very thing God set apart to signify a life given for a life — which is why Hebrews can say that without shedding of blood is no remission. Whatever a congregation concludes about eating black pudding, the reason for the reverence should not be lost, and the New Testament nowhere weakens it: we are redeemed not with corruptible things, but with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot.
roots_summary: Greek pniktos, strangled or choked — Acts 15:20, 29, 21:25; haima, blood; Hebrew nephesh, life or soul — Leviticus 17:11; dam, blood — Genesis 9:4.
roots_lines: Greek pniktos — choked, strangled; only in the three Acts references to the council's decree.
Greek haima — blood; the companion prohibition, and the word of the atonement in Hebrews.
Hebrew dam — blood; Genesis 9:4, in the covenant with Noah.
Hebrew nephesh — life, soul; Leviticus 17:11, “the life of the flesh is in the blood.”
Hebrew kaphar — to cover, to make atonement; the purpose God assigned to blood.
usage: “From things strangled, and from blood” — the two prohibitions belong together.
“Flesh with the life thereof… shall ye not eat” — given to Noah, before Sinai.
“It is the blood that maketh an atonement for the soul” — the reason underneath.
